title: Find the Largest Number
prompt: Given an array of numbers, return the largest one.

steps: Assume the first element is the largest so far.
Loop through the rest of the array, starting at index 1.
Whenever a bigger number appears, update your "largest so far" value.
After the loop ends, that variable holds the true maximum.
approach.example: For [3, 7, 2]: start with largest = 3. Compare 7 > 3 → update to 7. Compare 2 > 7 → no update. Final answer: 7.

walkthroughSteps: largest starts as numbers[0], giving the loop a baseline to compare against.
The loop begins at index 1, since index 0 is already accounted for.
Each iteration checks: is the current number bigger than largest?
If yes, largest is updated. If no, nothing changes.
After the final index, largest holds the maximum value in the array.
commonMistakes: Starting largest at 0 instead of numbers[0] — fails on all-negative arrays
Starting the loop at i = 0, redundantly comparing the first element to itself

title: Reverse a String
prompt: Given a string, return it reversed, without using the built-in .reverse() array method as a shortcut.

steps: Start with an empty result string.
Walk the original string backward, from the last character to the first.
Append each character to result as you go.
approach.example: For "cat": i=2 → 't', result='t'. i=1 → 'a', result='ta'. i=0 → 'c', result='tac'.

walkthroughSteps: The loop starts at str.length - 1, the index of the last character.
Each pass appends str[i] to result, then decrements i.
Because we're reading the string back-to-front, the built string comes out reversed.
The loop stops once i drops below 0, meaning every character has been visited.
commonMistakes: Starting at str.length instead of str.length - 1 — reads undefined on the first pass
Using result = str[i] + result instead of += — works, but is slower on large strings

title: Two Sum
prompt: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Assume exactly one solution exists.

steps: A brute-force check of every pair is O(n²) — too slow for large arrays.
Instead, walk the array once, using a hash map to remember numbers already seen.
For each number, compute its complement (target - number) and check if that complement is already in the map.
If it is, that's your pair. If not, add the current number to the map and keep going.
approach.example: nums=[2,7,11,15], target=9. i=0 (2): complement=7, not seen yet → store 2→0. i=1 (7): complement=2, IS in map at index 0 → return [0,1].

walkthroughSteps: seen maps a number to the index where it appeared.
Before adding the current number, its complement is checked against the map first.
That ordering matters: checking before adding prevents a number from pairing with itself.
If a match is found, the stored index and the current index are returned immediately.
commonMistakes: Adding nums[i] to the map before checking for the complement — can wrongly pair a number with itself
Using a plain object instead of a Map — works for integer keys but Map is the clearer, safer choice

title: Reverse a Linked List
prompt: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse it in place and return the new head.

steps: Walk the list once, keeping track of the previous node (starts as null).
At each node, save a reference to the next node before it gets overwritten.
Point the current node's next backward, at prev.
Advance both prev and current forward by one node.
approach.example: For 1→2→3: after all iterations the pointers flip to 1←2←3, and prev ends on node 3 — the new head.

walkthroughSteps: next is saved first because current.next is about to be overwritten — without saving it, the rest of the list would be lost.
Each iteration flips exactly one pointer to point backward.
prev and current both advance forward, one node at a time.
When current becomes null, prev is sitting on the last node visited — the new head of the reversed list.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to save next before reassigning current.next — loses the rest of the list
Returning current instead of prev — current is null at the end of the loop

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
prompt: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring that has no repeating characters.

steps: Use a sliding window with two pointers, left and right.
Expand right one character at a time, tracking each character's last-seen index in a map.
If the current character was already seen INSIDE the current window, jump left forward past that previous occurrence.
Track the longest window size seen so far.
approach.example: For "abba": right=1 window=[0,1] 'ab'. right=2 'b' repeats inside window → left jumps to 2. right=3 'a' was seen at 0, but that's outside the window (left=2) → no jump. Max length stays 2.

walkthroughSteps: lastSeen.get(char) >= left checks whether the repeat happened INSIDE the current window, not just anywhere earlier in the string.
That check is exactly what prevents left from ever moving backward.
Moving left to lastSeen.get(char) + 1 skips past the duplicate directly, instead of shrinking the window one step at a time.
maxLength is updated every iteration by comparing against the current window size, right - left + 1.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the >= left check — jumps left backward on repeats from outside the window
Recomputing the window length with a nested loop instead of tracking it with left and right directly

title: Breadth-First Traversal of a Graph
prompt: Given a graph as an adjacency list and a starting node, return the nodes in breadth-first order.

steps: BFS explores a graph level by level, using a queue instead of recursion.
Start by queueing the start node and marking it visited.
Repeatedly dequeue a node, record it, and queue any unvisited neighbors.
Mark neighbors visited the moment they're queued — not when they're dequeued — to avoid queueing the same node twice.
approach.example: Graph: A→[B,C], B→[D], C→[D]. Start at A: visit A, queue B,C. Visit B, queue D. Visit C, D already visited so skip. Visit D. Order: A, B, C, D.

walkthroughSteps: Marking a neighbor visited at queue-time, not dequeue-time, is the key detail — otherwise the same node could be queued multiple times before it's ever processed.
queue.shift() removes from the front, so nodes are processed in the order they were discovered.
That discovery order is what gives BFS its level-by-level property.
The loop ends once the queue is empty, meaning every reachable node has been visited.
commonMistakes: Marking visited only when a node is dequeued — allows duplicate entries in the queue
Using queue.pop() instead of queue.shift() — that turns it into DFS, not BFS

title: Sum of Array Elements
prompt: Given an array of numbers, return the sum of all elements.

steps: Start a running total at 0.
Loop through the array once.
Add each element to the running total.
Return the total after the loop ends.
approach.example: For [4, 1, 3]: total=0 -> 4 -> 5 -> 8. Final answer: 8.

walkthroughSteps: total starts at 0 so an empty array correctly sums to 0.
Each loop pass adds the current element to total.
No index tracking beyond i is needed since nothing is compared.
After the last element, total holds the full sum.
commonMistakes: Starting total at 1 instead of 0
Forgetting to return total

title: Find the Smallest Number
prompt: Given an array of numbers, return the smallest one.

steps: Assume the first element is the smallest so far.
Loop through the rest of the array.
Whenever a smaller number appears, update your tracked value.
Return that value after the loop.
approach.example: For [5, 2, 9]: smallest=5 -> 2 (2<5) -> stays 2. Final answer: 2.

walkthroughSteps: smallest starts at numbers[0], the same pattern as finding a maximum but flipped.
The loop starts at index 1 since index 0 is the starting baseline.
Each comparison checks for a strictly smaller value.
The final value of smallest is the minimum of the array.
commonMistakes: Using > instead of < by habit from a max function
Looping from index 0, comparing the first element to itself

title: Count Vowels in a String
prompt: Given a string, count how many vowels (a, e, i, o, u) it contains.

steps: Define a string of vowel characters to check against.
Start a counter at 0.
Loop through each character of the input string.
If the character is a vowel, increment the counter.
approach.example: For 'code': c-no, o-yes(1), d-no, e-yes(2). Final answer: 2.

walkthroughSteps: vowels.includes(char) checks membership in a small fixed set.
The loop visits every character exactly once.
count only increments on a vowel match, nothing else changes it.
Uppercase vowels wouldn't match here since vowels is lowercase only.
commonMistakes: Not handling uppercase letters if the input might have them
Using == instead of .includes for membership checking

title: Check Even or Odd
prompt: Given a number, return either the word even or the word odd depending on its parity.

steps: Use the modulo operator to find the remainder when dividing by 2.
A remainder of 0 means the number is even.
Any other remainder means the number is odd.
Return the matching string.
approach.example: For 7: 7 % 2 = 1, not 0, so return 'odd'. For 4: 4 % 2 = 0, return 'even'.

walkthroughSteps: % 2 gives the remainder after dividing by two.
Even numbers always leave a remainder of exactly 0.
The strict === avoids type-coercion surprises.
Any non-zero remainder falls through to the odd case.
commonMistakes: Using = instead of === for comparison
Forgetting negative numbers still work correctly with %

title: Average of an Array
prompt: Given an array of numbers, return the average (mean) value.

steps: Sum all the elements in the array using a loop.
Divide the total by the number of elements.
Return that result.
approach.example: For [2, 4, 6]: sum=12, count=3, average=12/3=4.

walkthroughSteps: The sum is computed with the same running-total pattern as before.
Dividing by numbers.length converts the total into a mean.
This assumes the array isn't empty, which would divide by zero.
The result may be a decimal, which is expected for an average.
commonMistakes: Dividing inside the loop instead of after it
Not guarding against an empty array in production code

title: Check Palindrome
prompt: Given a string, return true if it reads the same forwards and backwards.

steps: Use two pointers: one at the start, one at the end.
Compare the characters at both pointers.
If they ever differ, it's not a palindrome.
Move the pointers toward the middle until they meet.
approach.example: For 'noon': left=0 'n', right=3 'n', match. left=1 'o', right=2 'o', match. Pointers meet, return true.

walkthroughSteps: left and right start at opposite ends of the string.
Any mismatch immediately returns false, no need to keep checking.
left++ and right-- move both pointers toward the center each pass.
If the loop finishes with no mismatch, the string is a palindrome.
commonMistakes: Using left <= right, which double-checks the middle character unnecessarily
Forgetting to move both pointers each iteration

title: Count Character Occurrences
prompt: Given a string and a target character, count how many times it appears.

steps: Start a counter at 0.
Loop through every character in the string.
If the character matches the target, increment the counter.
Return the final count.
approach.example: For 'banana', target 'a': matches at index 1, 3, 5. Count = 3.

walkthroughSteps: The loop checks each character against target one at a time.
count only changes on an exact match.
This is case-sensitive, since === compares characters directly.
The final count reflects every matching position in the string.
commonMistakes: Case-sensitivity surprises when target case doesn't match the string
Off-by-one on the loop bound using <= instead of <

title: Find the Largest of Three
prompt: Given three numbers, return the largest of them.

steps: Compare the first two numbers and keep the bigger one.
Compare that result against the third number.
Return the final winner.
approach.example: For 4, 9, 2: max(4,9)=9, max(9,2)=9. Final answer: 9.

walkthroughSteps: largest starts as the first argument, a.
The first if checks b against the current largest, updating if bigger.
The second if repeats the same check against c.
By the end, largest has been compared against every candidate.
commonMistakes: Using else if instead of two separate ifs, which skips a needed comparison
Assuming the largest input position without actually comparing

title: Capitalize First Letter
prompt: Given a lowercase word, return it with the first letter capitalized.

steps: Take the first character of the string.
Convert just that character to uppercase.
Combine it with the rest of the string unchanged.
Return the combined result.
approach.example: For 'hello': first char 'h' -> 'H'. Rest is 'ello'. Result: 'Hello'.

walkthroughSteps: word[0] grabs only the first character of the string.
toUpperCase() converts that single character.
slice(1) returns everything from index 1 onward, unchanged.
Concatenating the two pieces rebuilds the full capitalized word.
commonMistakes: Calling toUpperCase() on the whole word instead of just the first letter
Off-by-one in slice, using slice(0) which re-includes the first letter

title: Sum of Digits
prompt: Given a positive integer, return the sum of its digits.

steps: Start a total at 0.
Repeatedly take the last digit using n % 10.
Add that digit to the total, then remove it using integer division.
Stop once the number reaches 0.
approach.example: For 123: digit=3, total=3, n=12. digit=2, total=5, n=1. digit=1, total=6, n=0. Stop.

walkthroughSteps: n % 10 always extracts the current last digit of n.
Math.floor(n / 10) removes that digit by shifting everything right.
The loop continues until n has no digits left to peel off.
total accumulates each digit as it's extracted.
commonMistakes: Using n / 10 without Math.floor, leaving a decimal
Not handling n = 0 as an input, which correctly returns 0 here

title: Factorial of a Number
prompt: Given a non-negative integer n, return its factorial (n!).

steps: Start a result at 1 (the identity for multiplication).
Loop from 1 up to and including n.
Multiply result by each number in that range.
Return the final product.
approach.example: For 4: result=1*1=1, *2=2, *3=6, *4=24. Final answer: 24.

walkthroughSteps: result starts at 1, not 0, since multiplying by 0 would zero everything out.
The loop runs from 1 through n inclusive, using <=.
Each pass multiplies the running result by the current i.
When n is 0, the loop body never runs and result correctly stays 1.
commonMistakes: Starting result at 0 instead of 1
Using < instead of <=, which skips multiplying by n itself

title: Check for Prime Number
prompt: Given a number greater than 1, return true if it is prime.

steps: Loop from 2 up to (but not including) the number itself.
If any of those values evenly divides the number, it isn't prime.
If the loop finishes with no divisor found, the number is prime.
approach.example: For 7: check 2,3,4,5,6 — none divide evenly. Prime. For 8: 2 divides evenly. Not prime.

walkthroughSteps: The loop starts at 2, since checking 1 or the number itself is pointless.
num % i === 0 means i divides num with no remainder.
Finding even one such divisor is enough to return false immediately.
Reaching the end of the loop with no divisor found means num is prime.
commonMistakes: Starting the loop at 1, which always divides evenly and breaks the logic
Not handling num <= 1 as a special case in production code

title: Remove Duplicates from Array
prompt: Given an array, return a new array with duplicate values removed.

steps: Create a Set from the array — Sets only keep unique values.
Spread the Set back into a new array.
Return that array.

walkthroughSteps: new Set(arr) builds a collection that automatically drops repeated values.
Sets preserve the original insertion order of first appearances.
The spread operator ... unpacks the Set's values into a plain array.
The result contains each original value exactly once.
commonMistakes: Forgetting Sets aren't arrays, and need spreading or Array.from to convert back
Assuming order isn't preserved, when it actually is

title: Find Index of a Value
prompt: Given an array and a target value, return the index of its first occurrence, or -1 if not found.

steps: Loop through the array with an index variable.
Compare each element to the target.
Return the index the moment a match is found.
If the loop finishes with no match, return -1.
approach.example: For [5, 8, 2], target 8: index 0 is 5 (no match), index 1 is 8 (match) -> return 1.

walkthroughSteps: The loop checks each index in order, starting from 0.
Returning immediately on a match guarantees the FIRST occurrence is found.
If nothing matches by the end of the array, -1 signals that nothing was found.
This is the same idea behind the built-in Array.indexOf method.
commonMistakes: Returning true/false instead of the index itself
Continuing the loop after finding a match instead of returning right away

title: Count Even Numbers in Array
prompt: Given an array of numbers, count how many of them are even.

steps: Start a counter at 0.
Loop through the array.
Check each number's remainder when divided by 2.
Increment the counter for every even number found.
approach.example: For [1, 2, 3, 4]: 2 and 4 are even. Count = 2.

walkthroughSteps: The loop visits every number in the array exactly once.
numbers[i] % 2 === 0 is the standard even-number check.
count only increases on a true even check, nothing else touches it.
The final count reflects the total even numbers found.
commonMistakes: Checking % 2 === 1 for even by mistake, which actually tests odd
Incrementing count outside the if block, counting every element

title: Reverse an Array
prompt: Given an array, return a new array with the elements in reverse order, without using the built-in .reverse() method.

steps: Create an empty result array.
Loop through the original array from the last index to the first.
Push each element into the result array as you go.
Return the result.
approach.example: For [1, 2, 3]: push 3, push 2, push 1. Result: [3, 2, 1].

walkthroughSteps: The loop starts at the last valid index, arr.length - 1.
Each pass pushes the current element onto result, then decrements i.
Reading arr back-to-front while pushing forward builds the reverse.
The loop stops once i drops below 0.
commonMistakes: Starting at arr.length instead of arr.length - 1
Using unshift instead of push, which works but is much slower

title: Check if Array Contains a Value
prompt: Given an array and a target value, return true if the array contains it, without using .includes().

steps: Loop through every element in the array.
Compare each element to the target.
Return true immediately on a match.
If the loop finishes with no match, return false.
approach.example: For [3, 7, 1], target 7: index 0 is 3 (no), index 1 is 7 (match) -> return true.

walkthroughSteps: This is the same scanning pattern as findIndex, just returning a boolean.
Returning true early avoids scanning the rest of the array unnecessarily.
false is only reached if every element has been checked with no match.
This is exactly what the built-in .includes() does internally.
commonMistakes: Returning arr[i] instead of true, which returns the wrong type
Setting a flag variable instead of returning directly, adding unneeded complexity

title: Find the Longest Word
prompt: Given an array of words, return the longest one.

steps: Assume the first word is the longest so far.
Loop through the rest of the words.
Compare each word's length to the current longest.
Update and return the longest word found.
approach.example: For ['cat', 'elephant', 'dog']: longest='cat'(3) -> 'elephant'(8, bigger) -> stays 'elephant'.

walkthroughSteps: longest starts as the first word, giving a baseline to compare.
The loop compares .length, not the words themselves.
Whenever a longer word appears, longest is reassigned to it.
This is the same max-tracking pattern as finding the largest number.
commonMistakes: Comparing words[i] > longest directly, which compares alphabetically not by length
Forgetting .length on one side of the comparison

title: Count Positive Numbers
prompt: Given an array of numbers, return how many values are greater than zero.

steps: Start a counter at zero.
Visit each number in the array.
Increase the counter when the number is positive.
Return the final count.
approach.example: For [-2, 4, 7, 0, -1], the counter becomes 1 after 4, then 2 after 7, so the result is 2.

walkthroughSteps: count stores how many positive values have been found.
The loop checks every value in numbers.
Only values greater than zero increase count.
The final count is returned after the full array is processed.
commonMistakes: Counting zero as a positive number.
Returning the counter before the loop finishes.

title: Count Negative Numbers
prompt: Given an array of numbers, return how many values are less than zero.

steps: Initialize a counter to zero.
Check each number in the array.
Increase the counter for every negative value.
Return the counter.
approach.example: For [3, -4, -2, 8, -1], the counter reaches 1, then 2, then 3, giving a result of 3.

walkthroughSteps: count begins at zero because no values have been checked.
The loop examines every number exactly once.
A number below zero causes count to increase.
The completed count is returned.
commonMistakes: Using > 0 instead of < 0.
Counting zero as a negative number.

title: Multiply Array Elements
prompt: Given an array of numbers, return the product of all its elements.

steps: Start the product at one.
Visit each number in the array.
Multiply the running product by the current number.
Return the final product.
approach.example: For [2, 3, 4], the product changes from 1 to 2, then 6, then 24, so the result is 24.

walkthroughSteps: product starts at one so the first multiplication keeps the value unchanged.
Each loop iteration multiplies product by the current number.
The running value therefore contains the product of all processed elements.
The final product is returned.
commonMistakes: Starting product at zero and making every result zero.
Adding the numbers instead of multiplying them.

title: Count Odd Numbers
prompt: Given an array of integers, return the number of odd values in the array.

steps: Initialize a counter at zero.
Check each number using the remainder operator.
Increase the counter when the remainder is not zero.
Return the final count.
approach.example: For [2, 5, 8, 9], 5 and 9 have a remainder of 1 when divided by 2, giving a count of 2.

walkthroughSteps: count records the number of odd values found.
The loop checks every number with % 2.
An odd integer leaves a non-zero remainder.
The final counter is returned.
commonMistakes: Using === 0 and counting even numbers instead.
Checking number / 2 instead of number % 2.

title: Double Each Number
prompt: Given an array of numbers, return a new array where every value is multiplied by two.

steps: Create an empty result array.
Visit each number.
Multiply the number by two.
Add the doubled value to the result.
approach.example: For [2, 5, 7], the transformed values are 4, 10, and 14, producing [4, 10, 14].

walkthroughSteps: doubled stores the transformed values without changing numbers.
The loop visits each input value once.
number * 2 creates the transformed value.
push appends each transformed value to doubled.
commonMistakes: Changing the original array instead of creating a result.
Using number + 2 instead of number * 2.

title: Filter Even Numbers
prompt: Given an array of integers, return a new array containing only the even values.

steps: Create an empty result array.
Check every number for evenness.
Add even numbers to the result.
Return the filtered array.
approach.example: For [1, 4, 7, 8, 10], the values 4, 8, and 10 pass the even check, producing [4, 8, 10].

walkthroughSteps: evens stores only values that pass the condition.
Each number is tested with number % 2.
A remainder of zero means the value is even.
Matching values are appended to evens.
commonMistakes: Using !== 0 and returning odd values.
Removing values from the original array while iterating.

title: Replace Spaces
prompt: Given a string, return a new string with every space replaced by a hyphen.

steps: Start with the original string.
Find every space character.
Replace each space with a hyphen.
Return the transformed string.
approach.example: For 'hello world again', each space becomes a hyphen, producing 'hello-world-again'.

walkthroughSteps: text contains the original string.
replaceAll searches for every space rather than stopping after one.
Each matched space is replaced with a hyphen.
The transformed string is returned without modifying the original string.
commonMistakes: Using replace and changing only the first space.
Replacing spaces with an empty string and removing the separators.

title: Convert To Uppercase
prompt: Given a string, return the same text with all alphabetic characters converted to uppercase.

steps: Receive the input string.
Use the string uppercase conversion method.
Keep the resulting transformed value.
Return the uppercase string.
approach.example: For 'JavaScript', converting the string produces 'JAVASCRIPT'.

walkthroughSteps: text stores the input value.
toUpperCase creates an uppercase version of the string.
The original string is not changed because strings are immutable.
uppercaseText is returned to the caller.
commonMistakes: Writing toUppercase instead of toUpperCase.
Expecting the original string variable to change automatically.

title: Trim Text
prompt: Given a string, remove whitespace from the beginning and end and return the cleaned string.

steps: Receive the text value.
Remove leading whitespace.
Remove trailing whitespace.
Return the cleaned text.
approach.example: For    hello world   ', trimming removes the outer spaces and produces 'hello world'.

walkthroughSteps: text contains the original input including surrounding whitespace.
trim removes whitespace from both ends.
The internal space between words remains unchanged.
cleanedText contains the returned result.
commonMistakes: Using replace to remove only one space.
Removing all spaces including spaces between words.

title: Check Starts With
prompt: Given a string and a prefix, return true if the string begins with that prefix and false otherwise.

steps: Receive the string and prefix.
Compare the beginning of the string with the prefix.
Use the boolean result of the comparison.
Return that result.
approach.example: For 'javascript' and 'java', the string begins with the prefix, so the result is true.

walkthroughSteps: text is the value being tested.
prefix is the required starting sequence.
startsWith checks whether prefix occurs at the beginning.
The resulting boolean is returned directly.
commonMistakes: Using includes, which allows the prefix to appear anywhere.
Checking the end of the string instead of the beginning.

title: Check Ends With
prompt: Given a string and a suffix, return true if the string ends with that suffix and false otherwise.

steps: Receive the string and suffix.
Check the ending portion of the string.
Use the boolean result of the check.
Return the result.
approach.example: For 'photo.png' and '.png', the string ends with the suffix, so the function returns true.

walkthroughSteps: text contains the string being tested.
suffix contains the required ending.
endsWith checks whether suffix matches the end of text.
The boolean result is returned directly.
commonMistakes: Using startsWith and checking the wrong side.
Using includes and accepting suffixes that occur in the middle.

title: Join Array Words
prompt: Given an array of words, combine them into one sentence with a single space between each word.

steps: Receive the array of words.
Use a space as the separator.
Join the array elements in their existing order.
Return the resulting sentence.
approach.example: For [I, learn, JavaScript], joining with spaces produces I learn JavaScript.

walkthroughSteps: words contains each individual word.
join uses a single space as the separator.
The words remain in their original array order.
sentence stores the completed string.
commonMistakes: Using join('') and removing all spaces between words.
Adding a trailing space manually after every word.

title: Split Sentence
prompt: Given a sentence containing words separated by spaces, return an array containing each word.

steps: Receive the sentence string.
Use a space as the separator.
Split the sentence into individual words.
Return the resulting array.
approach.example: For learn JavaScript daily, splitting on spaces produces [learn, JavaScript, daily].

walkthroughSteps: sentence contains the complete input text.
split searches for each space separator.
Each separated section becomes one array element.
words is returned as the collection of individual words.
commonMistakes: Using split('') and getting individual characters.
Forgetting to provide the space separator.

title: Get First Array Element
prompt: Given an array, return its first element. Return undefined naturally when the array is empty.

steps: Receive the input array.
Access the element at index zero.
Store the accessed value.
Return that value.
approach.example: For [red, blue, green], index 0 contains red, so the result is red.

walkthroughSteps: Arrays use zero-based indexing.
items[0] therefore refers to the first position.
firstItem stores whatever value exists at that position.
The stored value is returned.
commonMistakes: Using items[1] and returning the second element.
Trying to use firstItem() as though it were a function.

title: Get Last Array Element
prompt: Given an array, return its last element.

steps: Find the array length.
Calculate the final valid index.
Access the value at that index.
Return the last value.
approach.example: For [10, 20, 30], the length is 3, so index 2 contains the final value 30.

walkthroughSteps: items.length gives the number of elements.
The last valid index is one less than the length.
lastIndex therefore points to the final element.
That element is returned from the array.
commonMistakes: Using items.length directly as an index.
Forgetting that JavaScript arrays start at index zero.

title: Copy An Array
prompt: Given an array, return a new array containing the same elements without reusing the original array reference.

steps: Receive the original array.
Create a shallow copy of its elements.
Keep the new array separate from the original reference.
Return the copied array.
approach.example: For [1, 2, 3], spreading the array creates another array containing 1, 2, and 3.

walkthroughSteps: items refers to the original array.
The spread operator copies its elements into a new array.
copiedItems therefore has a different array reference.
The new array is returned.
commonMistakes: Writing const copiedItems = items and only copying the reference.
Using the spread operator incorrectly outside an array literal.

title: Find First Match
prompt: Given an array of numbers and a target value, return the first number that equals the target, or undefined if none exists.
